utterances.text: For example, from one part of the Teslic or Doboj municipality there would come requests for moving out from the area, and immediately thereafter, or immediately after allowing Bosniaks and Croats to leave the area, there would ensue bombing of that area by those to whom I referred to as the Ustasha formations and Green Berets in my report. I didn't want to refer to them in any other way, any differently than what they called themselves. By doing so, we wanted to show that there was a certain link between some parts of municipalities, that there was some contact between them and the enemy side in the sense that they were exchanging information between themselves, and this is why we wanted to inform about this in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To summarise your position and the information you conveyed in your report is that this moving out had been coordinated with certain military operations that would typically ensue after the population had moved out.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the very beginning of your answer, you said that there was a request coming from civilians to move out.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There were even centres established to process and forward such requests. Most often those requests were approved so that people could leave the area, literally speaking, whenever they wanted. At one time, whoever wanted to leave could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, despite the circumstances that existed at the time, that it was wartime and so on, according to your information, there was a co-ordinated strategy in place, whereby the population would first ask to move out, following which, there would be an attack, either by Ustasha forces or the Green Berets, as you referred to them.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this happened very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, it is a fact, isn't it, that this report of yours pertains to Teslic municipality.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Doboj as well, I think. Yes, Doboj. In the wider area of Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, and what is written in your report, this was not an isolated incident typical for this particular municipality. Rather, everywhere, throughout the area there were similar scenarios taking place. By saying this, I'm referring to this request by civilians to move out, following which, there would be an attack by Ustashas or Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, none of the municipalities in the Banja Luka area, Doboj area experienced anything different than what I described. Mostly there would be transports, buses organised so that people could go where they wanted to go. People mostly went to the territory of the nowadays Federation, and there were certain crossing points agreed between authorities where these convoys would be let through. Bosniaks and Croats, a large number of them, went towards Croatia. In the same way they submitted a request to move out and then a schedule was determined, the date, the hour, the items they could take with them, and what they needed to do before they moved out. So the situation was identical in all of these areas. The fiercest bombing came from Ustashas and Green Berets in Teslic, Doboj -- Doboj, Samac area and so on. There were cases where 3.000 shells were fired in some areas in a single day. I'm just giving you this example as an illustration of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood your position well, this departure of civilians was voluntary within that scenario. The civilians withdrew, following which there would be an artillery attack. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did. But I want to give another observation, Mr. Zecevic. When you say "voluntary," yes, it was voluntary, but you have to bear in mind that the fact that there was a war going on certainly had its affect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of my question, if you remember, I stated that there were wartime conditions in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, when you proposed to the witness that the civilians population left the areas in which they had lived, following which there would be a bombardment or an artillery attack of the area, which populations are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that the witness was talking about the Bosniaks and Croats and they would pull out of the certain -- certain part of the territory, where, after their -- their departure, the artillery of the Bosniak and Croatian forces will attack that particular part of the territory. That is my understanding and we can ask the witness [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And that's also the understanding that I got. But I was just surprised to discover -- I was surprised about this because I would wish to discover the reasons why the Croat and Muslim forces would attack the areas where their own population had lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the Honourable Judge's question. Let me not repeat it. Perhaps you can just reply.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can. This referred to the territories and areas of those municipalities where there were mixed populations. There were both Bosniaks and Croats and Serbs. And, of course, this did not relate to Stenjak and Teslic, where Bosniaks lived in a vast majority. Some 99 per cent of the population was Bosniak. But this related to certain areas of the town where the ethnic groups were approximately equally present, all of them, Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. And, in my view, that's quite logical, and that it is logical what was my position in 1992 as well, because this report is not based on one single event, but, rather, a number of incidents of the same type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, just to be sure, would you be good enough to explain the logic to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. In a large number of municipalities that were not single -- that were not inhabited by predominantly one ethnic group, the populations were mixed or the ethnic groups lived very close to one another. For instance, in my town, my home town, Teslic, in the town itself, you could not really tell which ethnic group was in the majority, but the villages surrounding Teslic could be actually -- you could actually determine whether they were Bosniak or Serb or Croatian, and such villages were the ones that were shelled at least. Whereas, the greatest number of shells actually landed on the town of Teslic itself and you could see exactly the areas where these shells would land because in these areas where there was a mixed population, Bosniak, Muslim -- Bosniak, Croatian, and Serb, as a rule, they would -- Bosniaks and Croats would move out a few days prior to the event, and then a few days later, the shelling would start from those areas where Bosniaks and Croats were active and operating. And, again, I have to repeat, that they referred to themselves as Ustashas and Green Berets than was the terms that -- that was the term that I used as well. So as a rule, in those shellings, Serbs were victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the idea was that once the Muslims and Croats had moved out, the shelling by the Muslim or Croat forces was meant to drive out the remaining Serbs who lived there. Is that how we should understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you've understood me correctly, Your Honour. But I would like to add something. It wasn't their objective to drive them out, but, rather, to destroy them, to kill them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D284, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now please be shown, by way of illustration -- actually, a sample of your extended report information, document 2D02-1314, tab 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember it, or would you like me to show you the last page were your signature appears as well as the date?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I recognised the typewriter used. This was the typewriter that we used, and I do believe when you say that it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I would like you to tell us a few words about your report. You see in paragraph 2 -- or, rather, this report relates to the Prijedor municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be more specific, Kozarica in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you note here that with the help of the democratic action party, Muslim people in the area were issued 1.000 rifles. Here it says long barrels, but I assume that you are referring to rifles and similar weapons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also learned apparently that that number was far larger but it was your assessment that the -- this figure, 1.000, is about right; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received this information from several different sources. They were reliable sources, sources who had been SDB sources for many years and individuals of Bosniak ethnicity, and we considered this information reliable, especially because our collaborators of Bosniak ethnicity -- especially because of the fact that they were of Bosniak ethnicity, so we did not doubt that their information was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, in this information you point out the problem that you have already discussed here - let's not go back to that - where attention should be given to some individuals in smaller groups, Territorial Defence members, from the Republika Srpska area who cruelly treated citizens of Muslim ethnicity and so on and so forth. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you about here is something that you mentioned in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that will be on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where you say that it was your impression - that's in the second paragraph in English - "we are under the impression that the regular units and commanding officers of the Army of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina are impotent to deal with these individuals and informal groups which are fighting on the side of the Serbian people for their own personal gain." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You keep asking me whether I recall, do I remember, and I'm getting the impression that you think that I can't recall anything. I remember all this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You go on to say: "There is the serious danger that extremist individuals from one side may seize power and thus prevent the legal establishment of government." Now tell us, when you drafted this report did you have confirmation for this information that you set out here?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say here that you're under the impression that the regular units and commanding officers are unable put a stop to these individuals or informal groups, could you please just elaborate a little? What did you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I had good contacts with military security and active officers, active-duty officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army. I had good contacts with my colleagues from the public and state security in the Prijedor area, and through contacts with these people, I gained the impression that paramilitary units and groups at one point outnumbered the regular troops of the Republika Srpska Army and even some segments of the public -- public security service that was active in Prijedor and operating in Prijedor. Simply put, it was my understanding that the Republika Srpska Army, which was deployed in the area, did not do everything that it could because I always found it strange that if you had under your control a company-strong unit that you were unable to overwhelm a platoon, and especially so if you have under your control a brigade or a division, that you cannot arrest a small number, in percentage points that's a small number, of killers and criminals, and bring them to justice and in this way show that the greatest number of Serbian people, both those in uniforms and civilians, did not approve of such activities, and that is why I blame the army for this as well, if I am the one who can lay blame at anyone's door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason I asked you about this is because you said that they were impotent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry, I was wondering if you were -- if you could finish this off --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I think we can take the break now. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is ushered in, there was -- we had a short discussion about the -- the schedule for next week. Well, I informed Mr. Olmsted and Ms. Korner that it is my assumption that I would be, like, 30 per cent less than the time that I anticipated, so I believe -- I used 1 hour 40 minutes, plus this session, and I believe the first session in the morning on Monday, and I will finish my cross-examination, on assumption that I will tender these documents, as we agreed with the Prosecution. And it is my understanding that -- that the Zupljanin Defence required three sessions for cross-examination of this witness, which would enable us to have Mr. Riedlmayer on Wednesday, and we can guarantee that we will finish by Thursday, end of the working hours, with the Witness Riedlmayer. So the -- for this reason, we don't believe that the extra session is needed on Monday. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radulovic, you have before you document 1D03-3398. You can see it now on the screen before you. It is dated 5 June 1992 and signed Milos. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this report of yours?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You talk here about the personnel in the district prison, and you mention that out of eight employees, only one is a Serb while five are Muslims and two are Croats. This is on 5 June, 1992. Which district prison is this a reference to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just try to bring it up. I think this is in Doboj. Yes, this is the Doboj District Prison, because I never used the term correctional facility in Banja Luka. I did not use the term district prison for that prison, so this must refer to Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say eight employee, what do you mean by that? Do -- are you referring to guards there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is in the investigative department. I don't -- this is not a reference to the entire district prison but just to its investigative department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, according to this report, on 5 June, which is the date of the report, in the investigations department of the district prison in Doboj there were eight guards, five of whom Muslim, two Croats, and one Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to point out that this is a reference to the investigations department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said in my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D285.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see 65 ter 10192.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you see this report of yours dated 19 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Here you speak about Muslims and Croats leaving the area of Bosanska Krajina due to some propaganda, some false information; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was especially present in the areas of Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That false information, who spread it? Where did it originate from; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I do. The Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, unless there are objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, again, a small question just to be sure that I have understood this correctly. Why would the Bosnian and Croat side spread deliberately misinformation about a planned attack against them? What's the big idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give my comment. Your Honour, at the time when I wrote this, I did not make comments, or I didn't venture into assessments. After this much time, after all these years, I can state my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, if you would be so good. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The desire was to depict the situation in the territories controlled by the Serb authorities in -- in the media as unbearable for survival. And then various misinformation reached Bosniaks and Croats about the Serbs allegedly planning extensive military and other operations in those areas and that all Bosniaks and Croats would be killed. The objective was for these Bosniaks and Croats leave the areas they inhabited in Serb-controlled territory and cross over to the Muslim or Croatian-controlled areas with the overall aim of using it for propaganda purposes, and I can only repeat that the role of the mass media was very important at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise to the counsel. 65 ter number 10192 will become Exhibit 1D286.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it's also a fact, apart from the propaganda value, that this enabled Croat or Bosniak forces to get possible reenforcements from the ranks of these newly arrived individuals, reenforcements for their military units, right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you are now eliciting information which is not part of this report; however, the Milos Group did inform the relevant structures about that. These groups leaving for Croatia or for the Federation were a source of manpower for military units, so that your conclusion or assumption is, indeed, in line with the reality on the ground. And if I may add, the Bosniaks who went to Croatia created one of the strongest military units called the the Honorary Berber Platoon, who carried out offensive activities in the Gradiska municipality, which is part of the RS, and there have been instances of mass killings, both of members of the military and police units and civilians too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Tuesday, you gave evidence here, and yesterday, too, you testified that Mr. Kesic, who was chief of state security in Banja Luka, with regard to these reports of yours, as well as to the information you passed on to him orally, had a rather negative attitude. His opinion was that this information was not interesting for the service, that it is not significant, that the service shouldn't do anything about it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just point out something extremely stupid. On the list of the documents in possession of the OTP, there's also a report of the Milos Group from 1993, which is a report that we received from a high-ranking expert in the NATO forces that, namely, there would be a bombing of Serbia and Yugoslavia by NATO forces at a later -- at a certain point in time. However, this report was stuck in a drawer of Mr. Bera, who was constantly trying to devaluate my work and that of my group, and if you are siding with this Mr. Bera you are humiliating me because I have never been narcicisstic nor have I been a fool. .

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, that is not my intention at all. I would just like us to know what you know, and I hope that you will help us to achieve that. Such important information submitted by you in 1993 to your immediate superior as well as some previous information was not forwarded -- was not passed on; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I found out about that only later, that much of my information never made it to the people that should have received it. They never went further than the National Security Service in Banja Luka. And I can provide -- or I can corroborate this statement with facts because there is somebody in this very courtroom who can be a witness to what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Mico Stanisic for the first time in 1999. We met at the Intercontinental Hotel immediately after Arkan was killed. We wanted to sit exactly where he was killed. Somebody made a joke about that so we chose a different place to sit. And we spoke about the fact that my -- or, rather, I learned that much of my information that I had submitted never made its way to him. It seems to me that Mico Stanisic only changed his mind in 1999 because he seems to -- seems to have received information about me depicting me in a very negative light, but that is something that I heard not only from him but also from others; but these others don't matter because they have no connection with these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment of leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. It would seem that your answer has not been recorded in its entirety. If I remember well, you said it is only then that I understood that a large number of my reports never made it to him. Actually, not one did. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I am referring to these most important reports and the most complex information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want a full answer? So -- because for my sake I would like to give you a complete answer. I understood after the end of the war many of my reports were edited and changed to suit the expectations of their consumers. Sometimes they were toned down, sometimes they were amplified, and the key roles in that process were those of Vojin Bera and Nedeljko Kesic. I'm taking about the reports that were made for the RS. But this sort of editing couldn't be applied to the reports that went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It couldn't because you submitted such information directly to Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the facts that you have related to us just now were something that you learned about only after the war, right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among others, in the conversation with Mico Stanisic. But that was only one of the conversations with one of the persons after the war. I also learned about that in the conversation with Gojko Glickovic [phoen] toward the very end of the war or after the war. The man was surprised when we spoke, and he admitted to me that I was some sort of an idiot, a fool, that's the way I was presented to him while he was in a high position. So what I'm saying, this wasn't meant -- this wasn't done -- or, rather, it wasn't targeted at me. The purpose was to devalue the information that I passed on, not only about the crimes committed by Serbs because somebody didn't consider that suitable and they were covering it up. And that's the attitude they had to all security-related information, and everything was under a veil of secrecy or something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, the assistant minister for the SDB of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the first four months, from April to mid-August, that was a position filled by Slobo Skipina. It is a fact, isn't it, that you had no professional contact with Slobo Skipina throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was surprising to me, and I was also disappointed because Skipina and I had worked together in the SDB, and we did have contact previously, and I would have thought that he should have either accepted the information that I passed on or take steps against me if he believed that the information I submitted was a heap of rubbish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, he didn't do either of the two things because he didn't receive your information.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zecevic, that's the only justification of his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, sir, on page 10796 and further of our transcript here, you spoke about a report of yours dated 17th of May, 1992. In your testimony you said that the report was a result of your first information related to crimes committed by Serbian forces in Doboj by mid-May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not seeking confirmation, really, I just wanted to make sure that your answer was recorded properly in the transcript. It didn't occur originally, and I have about ten more examples, and I will just go through them to ask for your confirmation. On page 10814 of the transcript, you stated that some people had ID cards of the SNB or police without even knowing what kind of service that was.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that, unfortunately, the times were such, on page 10907, you spoke about paramilitary and para-police groups in Doboj having such ID cards. Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, but as I was saying before and I will repeat it, I described these groups as criminal organisations that weren't involved -- involved in the war for the interests of the Serbian people but for the purpose of looting, and to achieve that, they needed to kill people who possessed what they wanted from whom they wanted to take items and then they wanted to kill witnesses of their acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean just to get rid of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I admit I -- my terminology was a bit confused. The way you put it is much better. To get rid of a witness. A live witness is the worst witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When these paramilitary and para-police groups were discussed, these groups that you described as criminal organisations, you told the Prosecutor in response to his question when he asked you to enumerate them, but I presume because of the time-limits, you were interrupted, and I would like to ask you to now list paramilitary and para-police group that existed in Doboj in 1992.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something that can I ask you to ask the Trial Chamber for us to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the transcript page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. On page 10942 of the transcript, you said that some of the leaders in Teslic knew what the Mices had done and the crimes they had committed before even you were informed, and you mentioned, among others, the president of the court and the then public prosecutor in Teslic. The public prosecutor, for whom you claim that he knew what was going on in Teslic, was Mr. Peric; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Branko Peric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the next page of the transcript, 10943, do you remember, you were then shown an article from Slobodna Bosna, and you were asked to comment on it, and the Prosecutor suggested then that -- put it to you that your action followed only after the Mice Group began to commit crimes against Serbs as well, and that you -- or, rather, the group that you led only intervened because of that and not because they had committed the crimes against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would rather not say anything about this. This is absolutely untrue. It's a red herring, let me put it mildly. We intervened even earlier to protect Bosniaks and Croats. We intervened after those event, in order to protect Bosniaks and Croats. We intervened also, I mentioned the incident with the 600 Romas on that cross-roads, so this is very offensive to me and to my sense, my ethical beliefs, so nothing of that sort should be put to me. No one in this courtroom should put anything like that to me because I managed to keep my dignity in far worse situations than this. And if you allow me, I would like to take this opportunity to say something here. Somebody suggested here that I may feel uncomfortable testifying as a Serb against Serbs. I would just like to stress this: I'm not testifying against Serbs. I'm testifying about the events that I was a witness to and that I heard about, and I consider that those who committed those crimes were in no way related to me in any way, and that had nothing to do with them being Serbs, and that would not characterise Serbs. And if I were to make a choice between a human being and a Serb, I would always choose a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've actually pre-empted one of my questions. On the next page of the transcript, 10944, you testified about the situation immediately following the arrest of the Mices and the -- and you also talked about the group that you led in this operation. And you said that, at that time, the chief of the security services in Doboj, Mr. Bjelosevic and you, were on bad terms. And you said in the end that, according to you, he was not well-informed and did not know fully what these people had done. You concluded that based on a conversation with him; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Bjelosevic, as the chief of the CSB, from early May was resubordinated as a commander of a police unit to the army in the battle-field. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can tell you where exactly on the front line he was. He was in the operation zone that was fighting in order to try and break through the corridor, open up the corridor. And literally, he was, on a daily basis at the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said, in -- at the operations centre. Could you just tell us slowly what was the name of that operations centre or the place where it was?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the command, the operation centre at Duge Njive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said Duge Njive?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, the command centre at Duge Njive, was that the operative group command centre?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "Operational Group," I'm referring to the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, this location, the place where the operations centre was at Duge Njive, how far was that from Doboj or from Teslic? Can give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 70 kilometres from Teslic and about 30 kilometres from Doboj. Depends on the road you took. That, too, would make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The operation to break through the corridor, open up a corridor, were conducted in the course of the summer 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it took quite a while, so please don't ask me specifically at what point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Even after the corridor was established, road communication was very difficult all the way through August up until September.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even later. The road was often shelled from Orasje and Gradacac so you had to drive carefully and -- even after the corridor, conditionally speaking, had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have finished for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm pretty well near the end of my cross-examination, but I would like to stop here at three minutes so I can consult overnight and be able to focus my cross for tomorrow morning, in order to -- to save as much time as possible -- on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand what you mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was going to ask whether given there's a minute or so whether Your Honours had prepared to rule on the reconsideration application in respect of the articles. Which is either a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... well, not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Does it make any difference at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, Your Honour, but I know this is my pet thing, but we're building up again a lot of very compendious amount of -- of requests and motions and whatever that are unanswered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are painfully aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. So I was just wondering if something that was relatively simple could be dealt with, and could be dealt with by way of an oral ruling. But if Your Honours feel not, then I'm not pressing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We had prepared a ruling, but we still need to consider it one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will take the adjournment for the weekend and reconvene in Courtroom III on Monday morning. And I wish everyone a safe weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
